explanations.answer: Were they worse sinners than other Galileans
explanations.explanation: That's the question. Jesus asks, "Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way?" I think this one hurts, friend, because real people died here. He doesn't answer it with a shrug, either. He's about to say something that matters for everyone standing there.

explanations.answer: Did they offer the wrong kind of sacrifices
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but Jesus never asks about the sacrifices. Some of those present tell Him what happened, and He asks whether those Galileans were "…worse sinners than all the other Galileans…" That's the question He puts to them. I think this one is heavy, friend.

explanations.answer: Why did nobody try to stop Pilate
explanations.explanation: It's a fair thing to wonder, but Jesus doesn't ask it. Pilate comes up only because some of those present tell Jesus what happened (Luke 13:1). Jesus asks about the Galileans themselves: were they "…worse sinners than all the other Galileans…"? I think this one is heavy, friend.

Jesus says the opposite. He answers His own question with "No, I tell you." Those Galileans were not worse sinners than all the other Galileans. So the idea that they got what they had coming isn't what He teaches here.

Right, friend. Jesus says, "No, I tell you." Then He adds, "But unless you repent, you too will all perish." He doesn't agree that those Galileans were worse than the rest. He points the crowd to something else.

That's the word Jesus uses. He says, "But unless you repent, you too will all perish." And He says it twice, once about the Galileans and once about the eighteen under the tower (Luke 13:3, 5). When Jesus repeats something, I stop stirring and listen.

Praying is a good thing, friend, but it isn't the word Jesus says here. His words are "…unless you repent…" He says them in verse 3, and He says them again in verse 5. So the blank gets that one word.

Fasting is a real thing in the Bible, but Jesus doesn't bring it up in these words. What He says is, "But unless you repent, you too will all perish." Good guess for a quick answer, though. Next time, the word to look for is the one He says twice.

That's right. Jesus asks whether they were "…more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?" and He answers, "No, I tell you." I think this one is heavy, because eighteen people died when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them. Then He gives the same warning He just gave.

It's the other way around. Jesus says about the eighteen, "No, I tell you." They were not more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem. I think this is a heavy part, friend. What He says next is the warning about repenting.
Yep. The man "…went to look for fruit on it but did not find any." Not a little, and not some. The tree is planted in his vineyard, and that's where he looks.

That would be a different parable. Here the man "…did not find any." A few small figs? Friend, this tree didn't hand him even one. I'd settle for one lonely fig to show off like a trophy, but there wasn't even that.
No birds show up in this parable. The man "…did not find any." fruit to begin with. Nothing pecked and nothing picked, friend, because he found none.

That's it. The owner says, "Therefore cut it down! Why should it use up the soil?" It's a strong word to the keeper of the vineyard, and he doesn't soften it. Three years of searching and no fruit is how he gets there.

Moving the tree isn't what the owner says. His order is "Therefore cut it down!" He doesn't ask for a new field or a new spot. A tree that gets relocated instead of the ax would be the luckiest tree around, friend, but that's not in this parable.

The owner doesn't pass the tree along. Giving a neighbor a fruitless tree would be like regifting a lamp that doesn't turn on. What he actually says is, "Therefore cut it down!" The neighbor never comes into it.

Yes, a year. The keeper says, "Sir, leave it alone again this year." He doesn't argue that the tree deserves forever. He asks for one more round. And he speaks up for the tree right after the owner says to cut it down.
A month is shorter than what he asks for. The keeper says, "leave it alone again this year…" It's a year, friend, and later he even says "next year" (Luke 13:9). So the blank needs year, not month.
A decade is way too long. The keeper asks for "…again this year…" and then he talks about "next year." Ten years is a whole lot more than he asks for, friend. The word he uses is year.

explanations.answer: Dig around it and fertilize it
explanations.explanation: That's his plan. He says, “…until I dig around it and fertilize it.” He isn't just asking the owner to wait. He says he'll do the work himself during that year.

explanations.answer: Prune its branches and water it
explanations.explanation: Pruning and watering sound like good work, but the keeper doesn't say them. What he says is, “…until I dig around it and fertilize it.” Those two jobs are the whole plan in the text. Stick with his words, friend, and you'll be fine.

explanations.answer: Build a fence all around it
explanations.explanation: No fence in this parable. The keeper says, “…until I dig around it and fertilize it.” Digging and fertilizing is all he mentions. A fence never comes up.

No promise here. The keeper says, "If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down." He leaves both outcomes open. He asks for the time and says he'll dig and fertilize, but he doesn't guarantee fruit.

Right, he makes no promise. The keeper says, "If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down." Notice he says "if." He doesn't say what will happen, and the parable doesn't tell us either.
